In 2004, the FDA1 reviewed all reports that it had re- ceived, between 1969 and 2003, of serious adverse events in children (aged from birth to 16 years) given promethazine. Of 125 reports there were 38 cases of respiratory depression, ap- noea, or cardiac arrest; 29 cases of extrapyramidal dystonic reac- tions; 24 cases of other CNS reactions; 15 cases of seizures or seizure-like activity; 12 cases of dermatological reactions; and 5 cases of neuroleptic malignant syndrome. These reports included 22 cases of respiratory depression in patients aged 1.5 months to 2 years, 7 of which were fatal. Doses received in these 22 cases ranged from 0.45 to 6.4 mg/kg. Serious outcomes occurred with all routes of administration (oral, rectal, and parenteral). US li- censed product information for promethazine hydrochloride now contra-indicates its use in children under 2 years of age because of the potential for fatal respiratory depression; a strengthened warning regarding use in children aged 2 years and older advises use of the lowest effective dose and to avoid concomitant use of other drugs with respiratory depressant effects. UK licensed product information for phenothiazine antihistamines, such as promethazine and alimemazine, also warns that these should not be given to children under 2 years of age, and the BNFC advises that sedating antihistamines such as these should not be given to children under 2 years of age, except on specialist advice, be- cause safety has not been established. Concern has also been expressed about the safety in children of cough and cold preparations that contain antihistamines, cough suppressants, expectorants, and sympathomimetic decongest- ants, either alone or in combination. A systematic review2 has also found no good evidence for or against the effectiveness of over-the-counter preparations in acute cough. In early 2008, the FDA3 and MHRA4 both advised that over-the-counter cough and cold preparations should not be given to children under 2 years of age. They warn of the potential for serious and potentially life- threatening adverse effects and that such preparations provide only symptomatic relief, at best. If these products are used in children older than 2 years of age, the recommended dose should be followed carefully and measured accurately, and only one preparation should be used to avoid overdosage of the same drug or similar drugs. A review by the FDA of the use of such prepa- rations in older children (2 to 11 years of age) is ongoing. For the MHRA’s suggested management of the symptoms of coughs and colds, see Cough, p.1547. An association between phenothiazine antihistamines and sud- den infant death syndrome has also been investigated—see p.588. 1. Starke PR, et al.
